3. **`pain_point_evidence` enforcement gap between AC #2 and validator.** Plan AC #2 (line 197) requires: *"Every High-priority row has `pain_point_evidence:` populated with either public official evidence or explicit bounded language; corporate roots alone are not sufficient for High-priority outreach-fit claims."* The validator at `scripts/validation/validate_gtm_2554_matrix.py` REQUIRED_FIELDS (line 26) requires `pain_point_evidence` to be present, but the script contains no semantic check that it is *not* a corporate-root URL nor that its content differs from `corporate_root_evidence`. Without explicit SHA-injection in the prompt envelope, this AC is unenforceable for at least one of the three providers and will likely produce `UNAVAILABLE` artifacts that the plan itself disqualifies.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- **Context switching ≠ SMT/Hyper-Threading.** A context switch is an OS event: kernel saves one process's registers, picks the next runnable process, restores its registers. SMT is a hardware feature: two threads share one physical core's execution units *simultaneously*, with their own duplicated register files and instruction pointers. No OS swap, no register save/restore.
- **Disabling HT does NOT reduce context switches.** If anything, it can *increase* them — you go from 32 logical CPUs to 16, so the OS has fewer slots to park runnable threads. With Hermes + Claude + Chrome + browser tabs + background daemons all wanting CPU, more processes queue per core, and the scheduler has to swap them in and out more often.
- **What HT-off actually buys you (when it does):** each physical core's execution units, L1d/L1i cache, L2 cache, branch predictor, and TLB are no longer shared with a sibling thread. For a single tight numerical loop that's already saturating those units, exclusive access can mean 10–25% faster wall time. For code that stalls on memory or I/O, the sibling thread *helps* by hiding the stall — so HT-off makes it slower.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## Quick model: when HT-off helps vs. hurts

| Workload shape | HT-off effect | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Tight FP/SIMD loop fitting in L1 (e.g., dense matrix multiply, FFT inner kernel) | **+10–25%** | Both siblings would compete for the same FMA / SIMD units; giving one thread exclusive access removes contention |
| Memory-bandwidth-bound (large arrays, streaming) | ~0% | Bottleneck is DRAM, not execution units; freeing the sibling doesn't help |
| Latency-bound / lots of cache misses | **−10–20%** | Sibling thread was *hiding* the stall by running while the other waited on memory; remove it and the core just sits idle during misses |
| Many concurrent small jobs (your overnight 5-terminal batch) | **−15–30%** | You wanted those 32 logical CPUs as parking slots; reducing to 16 increases scheduler queueing and OS context switches — the opposite of what you asked about |
| I/O-bound (your current dominant case — FUSE/ntfs-3g) | ~0% | CPU isn't the bottleneck; you're waiting on the filesystem driver. Changing HT changes nothing |
